notes.note: Agents with tool access and no egress control are everywhere already. Something has gone wrong; the question is whether anyone says so.
Organisations barely disclose root cause for ordinary breaches. 'Our agent was manipulated' is a sentence nobody wants to be first to say.
Two years is long enough for one board to decide candour is cheaper than speculation.
Prompt injection is not speculative — it is a documented failure class with working exploits. Deployment is racing ahead of the controls.
Everyone is answering a different question. Attacker-side AI is excluded, and once you strip that out there is almost nothing left.
Copilots with mailbox and repo access are one misconfiguration from an incident, and plenty are one misconfiguration away today.
OAIC narratives are thin on cause. Even if it happens, the public record will say 'unauthorised access' and stop there.
Genuinely no idea. No base rate, no comparable, and the disclosure norms are being written as we go.
Vendors will describe it as a customer configuration issue, which keeps it out of the resolution criteria.
Someone will disclose it precisely because AI makes it newsworthy rather than embarrassing. The incentive runs the other way here.
Attribution to a specific system requires forensics most organisations do not do and would not publish.
I would take the other side of anything under 60%. Agent adoption in 2026 is faster than any control cycle I have seen.
